title: The site's own safety procedures and your supervisor come first
applies_when: Always. Whenever a step, a pack or Hadley says anything that differs from the site's own safety procedures, permits or the supervisor's instructions, the site wins.
words_shown: Your site's own safety rules and your supervisor's instructions come first. If anything here is different from them, follow the site, not this. Stop now. Go to your site supervisor or engineer.

title: A panel is live whenever light falls on it
applies_when: A step has you touch, cut, strip, open or test any wire, terminal or bare metal of a panel, a string or its wiring. A panel makes voltage in daylight, even in cloud, and its DC side stays live when the inverter or the mains is switched off.
words_shown: Stop. Treat every panel and its wiring as live in daylight. Switching off the inverter or the mains does not make it safe. Do not touch, cut or test it yourself. Go to your site supervisor or engineer.

lowered_for.words: You are signed off for meter tests: use a meter and test leads rated for the string's DC voltage, measure at the connectors, never across a loaded circuit.

title: Never pull connectors apart under load
applies_when: A step has you pull a panel's connectors, a string or a DC lead apart while current can flow. Pulling a connector apart under load can draw an arc that burns. Joining and plugging in connectors is daily work and is not a stop (Ghost, 2026-11-21).
words_shown: Stop. Do not part connectors yourself. Opening a pair needs the panel made safe first and the release tool made for it, and connectors pulled apart under load can spark and burn. Go to your site supervisor or engineer.

lowered_for.words: Before you part connectors, make sure no current can flow: turn the isolator off, or cover the whole panel. Then open each pair with the release tool made for it, never by hand. Never pull connectors apart under load: they can spark and burn.

title: Do not open an inverter, combiner, battery or other electrical enclosure
applies_when: A step has you open, unscrew or take the cover off an inverter, combiner box, junction box, isolator, fuse holder, battery cabinet, switchboard or any other box that holds wiring.
words_shown: Stop. Do not open this box. Parts inside can stay live and hold a charge even when switched off. Only someone authorised may open it. Go to your site supervisor or engineer.

title: Work at height or on a roof
applies_when: A step has you go onto a roof, a ladder, a scaffold or a frame, or near an edge, skylight or roof hatch, or carry a panel up. There is no safe height to fall from; the site sets the fall protection.
words_shown: Stop. Do not go up or near an edge until your supervisor has shown you the fall protection for this job and it is in place. Never climb a ladder carrying a panel. Go to your site supervisor or engineer.

lowered_for.words: You are signed off for work at height: do not go up or near an edge until the fall protection for this job is in place. Never climb a ladder carrying a panel.

title: Keep well away from overhead power lines
applies_when: A step has you work, lift a panel, raise a ladder or move a tool or machine anywhere near an overhead power line.
words_shown: Stop. Do not work, lift or raise anything near an overhead power line. It can kill without being touched. Stay at least 10 feet (3 metres) away, and farther for higher voltage, or the site's own distance if it is greater. Go to your site supervisor or engineer.

sources.title: OSHA: Green Job Hazards, Solar Energy, Electrical (keep at least 10 feet from overhead lines; library: osha-solar-electrical)
OSHA: 29 CFR 1910.333(c)(3)(i), selection and use of work practices (overhead lines: keep a safe distance, at least 10 feet for lines up to 50 kV, more above; library: osha-1910-s)
OSHA: 29 CFR 1926.1408, cranes and derricks in construction, power line safety (up to 350 kV; library: osha-1926-cranes-power-lines)

engineer_to_confirm: This rule is beyond the brief's list (added because OSHA names overhead lines among solar workers' electrical hazards). The audit of 2026-11-21 found the hazard real on solar sites: perimeter lines and service drops at the site, and OSHA's Fort Riley 2018 citation. The words now give the distance (at least 10 feet, OSHA 1910.333(c)(3)(i) and 1926.1408; the site's own distance if greater). Keep, change or drop.

title: Damaged, burnt, melted, wet or corroded parts
applies_when: A connector, cable, panel or box is cracked, cut, crushed, burnt, scorched, melted, discoloured, corroded, wet inside, or has copper showing. The triggers fire only on text that says such a part is there, not on a step that tells you what to look for.

title: Heat, a burning smell, smoke, sparks or arcing
applies_when: Anything smells of burning, smokes, sparks, crackles or shows an arc or flame. A humming inverter, or a panel that is hot in the sun, is normal and is not a stop.
words_shown: Stop. Step back and do not touch it. Keep others away. If there is fire or smoke, follow the site's emergency procedure. Go to your site supervisor or engineer.

title: An earth (ground) fault or an electric shock
applies_when: A device shows an earth fault, ground fault, insulation or isolation fault, or a protective device trips; or someone feels a tingle or a shock from a frame, panel or box. A fault can make metal live that should not be.
words_shown: Stop. Do not touch the frames, panels or boxes. A fault may have made metal live. If someone has had a shock, call for help and first aid at once, switch off the power if you can do it safely, and do not touch them while they may still be touching it. Go to your site supervisor or engineer. If you had the shock yourself, get medical attention even if you feel fine.

sources.title: Fluke: What is a DC ground fault in a PV system?
OSHA: Green Job Hazards, Solar Energy, Electrical (shock and burns when connecting panels)
Better Health Channel (Victoria, Australia): Electric shock (a person who has had a shock may appear unharmed but should still receive medical attention)

engineer_to_confirm: The first-aid sentence (call for help, do not touch a person who may still be touching something live) is common first-aid practice but none of the sources above states it; the site's own first-aid arrangements apply. Keep, reword or source it. The same goes for SR-08's line to follow the site's emergency procedure on fire or smoke. The last sentence (J-089, R13), medical attention for the person who had the shock themselves, is sourced to the Better Health Channel page for that clause only; Ghost's wording also said to stop work, step away, not touch it again and tell the supervisor, and no page fetched for J-089 states those, so they were left out (the rule's first words already say Stop and go to the supervisor).

title: A voltage above what a device is rated for
applies_when: The panels' voltage, or the string's, is or could be above the device's highest input voltage. A panel's voltage rises in the cold, so a string that fits on a warm day may not on a cold morning.
words_shown: Stop. Do not connect. Too high a voltage can destroy the device and start a fire, and panels give more volts when cold. Go to your site supervisor or engineer.

title: Batteries
applies_when: A step has you connect, disconnect or work on battery terminals, battery cables or a battery bank; or a battery is swollen, hot, leaking, hissing or smells.
words_shown: Stop. Do not work on battery terminals or cables, and keep away from a battery that is swollen, hot, leaking, hissing or smells. A battery can burn, explode or give off toxic gas, and it cannot be switched off. Go to your site supervisor or engineer.

lowered_for.words: You are signed off for battery and controller wiring: keep away from a battery that is swollen, hot, leaking, hissing or smells. A battery can burn, explode or give off toxic gas, and it cannot be switched off.

title: Never bypass or switch off a protective device
applies_when: A step has you bypass, bridge, remove, tape over or switch off a fuse, breaker, isolator, RCD, earth connection, shutdown switch or other protective device so that something works.
words_shown: Stop. Never bypass, bridge, tape or hold in a fuse, breaker or other safety device to make something work. Switching off is safe; overriding is not. Go to your site supervisor or engineer.

title: Connecting to the grid or a building's mains
applies_when: The worker asks to connect solar to the grid or to a building's mains supply, or to feed power in or net meter. This is work for a licensed electrician and usually needs the network operator's permission before it is connected.
words_shown: Stop. Connecting solar to the grid or a building's mains is work for a licensed electrician, and usually needs the network operator's permission. Do not do it. Go to your site supervisor or engineer.
engineer_to_confirm: Both sources are government pages from New South Wales and Wales, not from the country the pilot runs in. The claims are by country: a licensed electrician (NSW), the network operator's permission (NSW; Wales), and the words say usually because a small UK system may only need notice, not prior permission. Replace them with the national regulator's and network operator's pages for the pilot's country, and confirm who counts as licensed there.

lowered_for.words: You are qualified: get the network operator's approval before you connect to the grid or a building's mains.

sources.title: NSW Government: Guide to solar panels (installation must be by a licensed builder or licensed electrical contractor; you must get approval from the electricity network owner before connecting your solar system to the grid)
Welsh Government: Connecting on-site generation to the grid, technical note (distribution network operators must authorise all installation of generating stations and battery storage systems)
